Descriptive source: "បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្តបច្ចេកវិទា ប្រព័ន្ធអន្ទាក់គ្រប់គ្រងសត្វកណ្តុរនៅស្រែ" (Technology Practice Standard: Trap-Barrier System for Rat Management in Rice Fields), Department of Agricultural Extension, MAFF, with CARDI, February 2006.
text:
Because one Trap-Barrier System (TBS) is meant to protect roughly 10 hectares of surrounding rice fields, this source recommends organizing it as a community effort among the farmers who benefit, rather than one household building and running it alone.

Forming the group: select farmers whose fields fall within roughly 200m of the planned TBS location, ideally with input from local authorities. Participation should be voluntary and based on genuine interest, since the work requires consistent daily follow-through. A group typically has a leader (often the owner of the land where the TBS sits, or a farmer respected in the community) plus members, who together agree on how to share materials, labor, and responsibilities before building starts - covering who prepares the trap-crop nursery, who helps assemble cages and barrier, and who does the daily monitoring rotation. Groups following this system typically meet roughly every two weeks to discuss issues and coordinate.

Economics: building one TBS costs roughly $35-50 (USD), not counting shared community labor or locally-sourced materials. This source's cited research found the resulting protected yield could be worth over 3 tons of rice across the season - at the price levels cited in this source (roughly 400 riel/kg at the time of writing, i.e. very roughly $300 worth of rice), suggesting a substantial net benefit (roughly $250, by this source's rough estimate) once shared among the participating farmers, distributed loosely in proportion to how much yield gain each farmer's field saw from being near the TBS. Treat these dollar and price figures as illustrative and dated (2006) rather than current numbers.

Challenges in group implementation: disagreements on priorities or approach among members, uneven effort or perceived unfairness in dividing labor and benefits, some farmers' reluctance to participate in group work generally, difficulty for some farmers to see the concrete benefit until they've experienced it firsthand, and in this cultural context, some discomfort tied to Buddhist reluctance to kill animals. Uneven or unpredictable rainfall timing can also make it hard to coordinate the staggered trap-crop nursery schedule precisely as recommended. When local rat populations are very high, cages and barriers also take more physical damage and need more frequent repair, which can reduce trapping effectiveness relative to the size of the rat population.

Gender roles: both men and women can carry out TBS work, but in practice men more often do the heavier tasks - building cages and assembling the barrier - while women more often help prepare the trap-crop nursery, set up the barrier, and do daily monitoring and upkeep. Effective participation in a household typically depends on agreement between spouses on taking part.

Environmental effects: on the positive side, TBS is a mechanical/physical method that avoids rodenticide use entirely, which helps protect farmers' living environment and reduces reliance on other methods that can carry more risk to human and animal health. Cage traps sometimes catch beneficial non-target animals (e.g., certain snakes, frogs, crabs) along with rats; ideally these should be released unharmed, and they can also play a useful role in natural pest control around the field. On the negative side, this source notes that some farmers do kill beneficial animals caught in the cages for food, and that leftover plastic barrier fragments are sometimes left in the field after the season rather than properly collected, which affects local soil/field cleanliness though this source does not describe it as a severe environmental impact.
